title: Build a producer-consumer queue that does not corrupt
objective: By the end of this lesson you have written a bounded queue that several producers and consumers use concurrently, shuts down without losing items or hanging, and passes thread sanitizer.

blocks.text: This is the structure underneath thread pools, job runners, logging pipelines, and every server that separates accepting work from doing it. It uses everything in this module at once: a mutex for the data, condition variables for the waiting, and a shutdown protocol that is where almost every homemade version goes wrong.

items: Every item produced is consumed exactly once — none lost, none duplicated
A producer facing a full queue waits instead of overwriting: that is back-pressure, and it is the point of a bounded queue
A consumer facing an empty queue sleeps instead of spinning
When production ends, every consumer exits — after draining what is left, not before
No thread is left asleep at shutdown

blocks.caption: A bounded queue, complete
lines: pthread_cond_t not_full, not_empty;   /* two conditions, one mutex */
/* returns 1 with an item, or 0 when the queue is closed AND drained */
if (q->count == 0 && q->closed) {              /* the only clean exit */
pthread_cond_broadcast(&q->not_empty);   /* broadcast, not signal — see below */

blocks.title: Two conditions, one mutex — and why
blocks.text: Producers and consumers wait for opposite things, so they need separate condition variables: waking a producer because the queue became non-empty would be pointless. But both wait on the SAME mutex, because both are protecting the same data. One mutex per shared structure, as many condition variables as there are distinct things to wait for.
Shutdown: the part that is usually wrong

A consumer's wait condition is (count > 0 || closed). Without the second half, closing the queue leaves every consumer asleep with nothing to wake them, and the program hangs at exit — the failure the previous lesson warned about. And the wake-up must be a broadcast: signal wakes one consumer, that one exits, and the rest sleep forever.
The order also matters. Join the producers first, then close, then join the consumers. Closing while producers are still running would tell consumers to stop before the work is finished.

blocks.caption: Main, in the only order that works
lines: for (int i = 0; i < CONSUMERS; i++) pthread_create(&c[i], NULL, consumer, NULL);
for (int i = 0; i < PRODUCERS; i++) pthread_create(&p[i], NULL, producer, NULL);
for (int i = 0; i < PRODUCERS; i++) pthread_join(p[i], NULL);   /* 1. producers finish */
for (int i = 0; i < CONSUMERS; i++) pthread_join(c[i], NULL);   /* 3. consumers drain and exit */

blocks.text: How to know it is right

Do not judge it by whether it appears to work. Count. Three producers pushing 50,000 items each must produce exactly 150,000 consumed items, and the queue must end empty. Verified: five consecutive runs of this implementation reported 150,000 produced, 150,000 consumed, and count 0 — and thread sanitizer reported nothing.

blocks.title: Counting the results needs its own lock
blocks.text: Each consumer counts locally and adds its total to the shared figure once, under a separate mutex, at the end. Incrementing a shared total on every item would be the race from earlier in this module — and it would also make the statistics the bottleneck of the whole program.

blocks.title: Build it, then break it four ways
steps: Implement the queue above with 3 producers x 50,000 items and 4 consumers
Verify: total consumed == 150,000 and the queue ends empty, over five runs
Build with -fsanitize=thread and confirm it is silent
BREAK 1: change the consumer's while to if — run and watch it take from an empty queue
BREAK 2: change q_close's broadcast to signal — run and watch it hang with consumers asleep
BREAK 3: call q_close before joining the producers — watch items get lost
BREAK 4: remove '|| closed' from the wait condition — watch it hang at exit
For each break, use Ctrl-\ to force a core dump, or attach with gdb -p <pid> and run thread apply all bt to see exactly where each thread is stuck
blocks.expected: One correct implementation and four distinct failures, each with its own signature: corrupted counts, a hang with all consumers in pthread_cond_wait, lost items, and a hang at exit. Being able to look at a stuck program's backtrace and say which of these it is — that is the deliverable of this whole module.

cheatsheet: One mutex per shared structure; one condition variable per distinct thing waited for
Producer waits while full; consumer waits while empty — always in a while loop
Consumer wait condition must be (count > 0 || closed), or shutdown hangs
Close with broadcast, never signal — every consumer must be woken
Order: join producers, then close, then join consumers
Consumers must drain the queue after close, not exit immediately
Count per thread and merge once; a shared per-item counter is both a race and a bottleneck
Verify by counting across several runs, and run it under thread sanitizer

checkpoint.prompt: Why must q_close use broadcast rather than signal?

choices.B: Every waiting consumer must learn the queue is closed; signal wakes one and the rest sleep forever
choices.C: signal only works with a single mutex

checkpoint.explanation: Closing is a state change that concerns all waiters, not a single item that one waiter can take.

checkpoint.prompt: A consumer waits while (count == 0) and the queue is closed with items still in it. What goes wrong?

choices.B: The consumer never learns about the close and sleeps forever, so the program hangs at exit

checkpoint.explanation: The wait condition must include the shutdown state: while (count == 0 && !closed). Otherwise there is no event that can end the wait.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does the queue have two condition variables rather than one?

choices.B: Producers and consumers wait for opposite conditions; one variable would wake threads that still cannot proceed

checkpoint.explanation: Same mutex, because it is the same data. Separate condition variables, because 'not full' and 'not empty' are different events.

checkpoint.prompt: You close the queue before joining the producers. What is the effect?

choices.A: Nothing, if the queue is empty
choices.B: Consumers may exit while producers are still adding items, so work is silently lost
choices.D: The queue rejects further items automatically

checkpoint.explanation: Close means 'no more will arrive'. Saying that while more are still arriving makes it untrue, and consumers act on it.
